get_text: Dum-dum! Dum! Dum-baddum-dum! Dum-dum! CLASH! — Let the show begin!

Martial arts movies are the hallmark of an era. In other words, they are a thing of the past.
Audiences are drawn to newer, trendier stories as they gradually leave these played-out tales behind.
With the retirement of the final generation of actors capable of performing authentic moves on screen, these movies have also taken their final bow.
But Manna refuses to just stand by and watch her favorite thing fade from the spotlight.
Because her personal idol never gave up...
So she won't give up the fight, either.

It's to be expected, of course. Manna knows.
But just before she turns to leave, she looks resolutely at the entire crew in front of her and speaks:
"I... love martial arts movies, and I want more people to love them too! That's why I'll work hard to become the best actor I can be, and show everyone that martial arts isn't dead."
Silence fills the room as she speaks these words from the bottom of her heart.
"Thank you for giving me this opportunity."
With these polite parting words, Manna turns confidently and walks away.

"Hi, I'm here for the audition." Manna takes her candidate number and finds a seat in the corner of the audition room. The place is filled with people, and the lively atmosphere makes her heart leap with excitement. "Candidate 76, Manna." "Present!" "What's your specialty?" Manna strikes a clean Asking Hand stance. "Wing Chun." The crowd starts whispering. "What is Wing Chun?" "I think it's some kind of kung fu? There were old martial arts movies about it, if I recall correctly." "That was ages ago." "Does anyone even watch those movies anymore?" These discouraging whispers make Manna nervous. She feels them shake her body, disrupting the perfect stance that she's fighting to maintain. The director speaks again. "Do you... have any other specialty?" Manna freezes under their judging gaze. Her mind completely blank. "N-No." As expected, her honesty earns her the response: "You can go now, thank you. Please wait for our call."

Of course, she's still frustrated by it. Manna clenches her fists, unsure where to unleash this fire burning her up from inside.
Suddenly, she feels a warm hand over her head.
Manna looks up in shock, and sees the superstar wearing a familiar, gentle smile this time.
She unties the red tassel from her wrist, one that Manna knows by heart. It was the symbol of her most famous role.
Then, the superstar gently ties it to Manna's hair. In that moment, Manna finally sees those calloused, trembling old hands.

"I quite like martial arts movies now."
"Because you have freed me from being their 'undisputed champion.'"

"A pot of Pu'er tea and a basket of peach buns." Today, her order was ready even before she sat down. "You're not challenging me today. I'm challenging you." The actress looks up and sees a completely reenergized Manna. She smiles in return. "The pleasure is mine." "Hooh...!" Bang! Manna blocks the first strike. "Hooh hyah!" Pow! Manna blocks the second strike, too. "Hi-YAH!" The third strike comes... Boom. In the end, just like always, Manna loses.

All this, just to exchange a few moves with Manna after work.
The first time, Manna was taken down in one move. The second time, she was still taken down in one move. Same with the third, and the fourth.
"Zero progress" is how Manna would rate her performance. So, she just has to put more muscle into it...
"Hi-yah!"
Bang! Crash!
And once again, she's completely defeated by the superstar in just one move.
"Wing Chun isn't about brute force."

She's never said anything to Manna after their first spar.
Manna frowns and glares at her in complete defiance. Surprisingly, the perpetually-arrogant actress smiles at her ruffled young opponent.
Manna doesn't understand her smile. Is this what they call "acting skills"?

Naturally, she continues to visit the teahouse, provoking Manna, and delivering crushing defeats right after. Over time, just hearing an order for "Pu'er tea" and "peach buns" is enough to incite a fiery rage in Manna's heart.
She desperately wants to "win," even when she can't quite figure out where this defiance came from.
Without professional guidance, she can only rewatch those martial arts movies and study the spars frame by frame. She'd watch and lose, watch again and lose again. The cycle continues... Until one day, she finally realizes the secret in the fight scenes she knows inside out.
"Wing Chun isn't about brute force," she concludes.
Her superstar had told her the solution from the very beginning.

The actress that she "used to" admire didn't just walk away after defeating Manna in one move. Instead, she shows up like clockwork every day at the teahouse where Manna works.
Still, no one else recognizes her as the former martial arts superstar. Only Manna knows that this "big shot," who has gone from her favorite to her least favorite person, comes to the shop every day with intent. She'd order a pot of Pu'er tea and a basket of peach buns, and just observe Manna all day long.

Ring, ring—
Manna's phone rings just as her palm lands a strike on the wooden dummy.

"Hello, Ms. Manna. We're calling from the ██ production crew and..."
Time and time again, being told to "wait for a call" had always ended in rejection for her. But this time...
"We'd like to invite you to join the cast of our upcoming martial arts film."

"Hah!"
"Hooh!"
"Hooh hyah!"
"Hooh hyah — hah!"

Manna strikes the wooden dummy with all her might.
She's still working at the teahouse, but she no longer spaces out during her free time. Whether she was commuting, taking a break, or clocking out after work, she's always practicing to improve her Wing Chun.

"I really like you and your movies." Fighting her anxiety, Manna confesses her admiration. "Those martial arts movies?... A shame. I don't actually like them that much." Manna stares in shock as the star crosses her arms coldly, looking down at her fan with a dismissive sneer. "Why?" The why is supposed to be a demand, but it takes all of Manna's just to force out a hoarse whisper. Meanwhile, the star maintains her arrogant posture and holds out a hand toward Manna — the Wing Chun Asking Hand stance, and taking that stance means... It's a silent exchange between martial artists. Manna's heart sinks, and her body moves before she can speak.

The teahouse is silent for a few seconds, then erupts into thunderous applause. "Nice moves!" The crowd goes wild. The person who caught the teapot looks just like a star... Wait a minute... Manna takes a closer look, and sure enough, it really is her — the legendary martial arts star who had announced her retirement. However, even after the praises and appreciations from the crowd, and after the excitement has died down, no one here recognized her as the superstar of that bygone era. Just as she's about to slip away unnoticed, Manna swoops in and places herself right in front of the star. "You... you're that famous martial arts actress, aren't you?" The lady smiled. "You're the only one who recognized me." Manna never thought she'd actually get the chance to meet her personal idol up close one day. Despite her age, her perfectly executed moves and extraordinary presence feel like she'd just walked out of the screen. Manna knows that she hasn't changed a bit...

"Hot water coming through!"
A waiter weaves through the crowd, carrying a pot of piping hot tea.
In his hurry, he slips, and with a jerk of his arm, sends the pot of scalding tea flying through the air. He watches helplessly as it heads straight for an innocent customer's head—
Before anyone has time to react, a gust of wind moves through the crowd, leaps, and flips to catch the steaming teapot with perfect form.

"Wing Chun, ██. Good match." Manna likes working at this teahouse because it's the only old shop left that still plays corny, old-school martial arts flicks on a clunky TV in the corner. The actress on the screen still flawlessly executes her Asking Hands, Seeking Bridges, and Vertical Punches... even when no one's paying attention to these old relics playing on loop in the background of the bustling teahouse. "Manna! Dishes to table 5, please." "Coming!" For a time, life feels like it'll manage just fine without these old flicks. Manna would still live the exact same way, kept busy during work hours and spacing out in her free time...

"Hi-yah! Wing Chun, I await your instruction." Through diligent, persistent viewing and imitating, Manna learned to perfectly execute martial arts moves such as the Asking Hand, Seeking Bridge, and Vertical Punch, even without any professional instructions. Meanwhile... "Please let us welcome the undisputed champion of martial arts cinema..." Just as Manna had envisioned, her favorite actress had become the biggest, most dazzling star in the real world, too.

Young Manna would always grab a good spot and watch with her eyes glued to the screen until the credits rolled.
Among the many fantastic scenes, there was always an actress who didn't get much screen time, but whose fight scenes were absolutely spectacular. Whenever she was on screen, Manna would focus even harder, tracking her every move.
Her flawless punches, clean kicks, and stylish spins... Manna had a feeling that one day, the actress would become the brightest star on the silver screen.
And so, without even realizing it, Manna started imitating her martial arts moves and expressions.

The old projector clicks and clatters as the thick film reel begins to turn, casting scenes of places, people, and events onto the screen.
These films usually tell tales of wandering heroes protecting the weak and fighting the wicked with their martial skills, of how bravely they step forward to defend their homes and families in times of crisis, and how bittersweet and memorable their journeys end.
To the audience, these stories feel distant because the comforts of modern life make it impossible to truly empathize with the struggles of harder times. But at the same time, the audience is pulled in through intimate frames that render them witnesses to every beginning, middle, and end of the tales.

"Hooh!"
Manna only needs to see a move once to replicate it, so she knows how to perform the counter like the back of her hand...
Bam! Crash!
Everything falls silent in an instant. With just one move, her opponent counters her and pins her in place.

"Do you see now?"
"..."
"Nobody but me could ever be the lead of a martial arts movie again, and I do not like being the 'undisputed champion' of things."

"Grab your stools and take the front row!"
At the sound of the gongs and drums, people start flooding in, converging from every street and alley.
A golden gust of wind moves through the crowd. It leaps, flips, then sticks a perfect landing in an uncontested best viewing spot for the movie.

It was the day before Medowlyn's coming-of-age ceremony.
When the maids pushed open the door, they found her already at work, putting the final touches on her preparations for the Coiffure Ball.
As the tradition required, her hair was styled to perfection—
Not a strand out of place. Neither one too many, nor one too few.
get_storytitle: Before the Ball, Not a Strand Out of Place

get_text:
For those who had already come of age, the PuffPost Boxes by their doors had been filling up lately. From time to time, a soft, fluffy gift would arrive from the Starsea.

"Ms. Ellie, a floofy violin won't snap, right? Shh... that lullaby is our little secret."
Ellie, the maid, smiled at the parcel. Even with one string missing, little Lynn would always play along, drifting off with a grin to the off-key tune.

"Cecily, the funny-faced bread tastes good too! After eating it... you'll get a funny face!"
Cecily of the Tulip family glanced at the bread plushie in the corner, remembering that camping trip with Lynn, when they burned the bread and hurriedly ate it all before anyone could notice.

"Anna, remember when the clam snapped open and splashed us with mud? And there was nothing inside!"
Anna, Medowlyn's former deskmate, carefully opened the plush clam in her hands. This time, soft little pearls nestled inside, giggling quietly.

Out in the Starsea, a small figure walked on, her eyes wide with wonder. Her once-cropped curls had begun to grow back, and this time, she no longer felt the need to keep them so carefully in place. Imperfection... really isn't such a bad thing. The open wind slipped freely through every soft strand of her hair. And somewhere in the distance... There must be even more beautiful memories waiting to be found, right? How lovely it will be to tuck them away in something soft and floofy.

The Coiffure Ball... might never be quite so perfect again.

Three days later, Judge Lucy sat at her desk, snapping her ruler and protractor apart, piece by piece, along the precise markings once used to measure the length and curve of every coiffure.

They said the girl had left without taking any of her hair accessories. Only a pair of scissors and some thread.

Had she truly gone?

Meanwhile, outside Medowlyn's room, her lady's maids were in a panic. The bell had rung three times, and at last the head maid, steeling herself, forced the door open.

Inside... the room was empty? Only an empty plushie box lay in plain sight.

A faint glimmer flickered at the windowsill, and as the maid stepped closer, she saw a fall of golden hair slipping softly down from the edge of the window, silken, luminous... and severed.

"Medowlyn from the Lucerne family's taking the Golden Comb this year, isn't she?"
"I mean, obviously. I heard the council's already saved her a seat, just waiting for her to claim it!"
"Ugh, I can't wait to see it..."

As the chimes sounded before the Golden Hall, the ball commenced. Young debutantes, each with a flawlessly arranged coiffure, entered the ballroom in pairs and trios.

"I'm done!" the little girl giggled, as if trying to shake the dirt from herself with laughter alone. In her hands was a lopsided, goofy-looking flowerpot... or perhaps a plushie? Its face was caught somewhere between a smile and a sob, just like the strange little ones Medowlyn had seen earlier in the garden. The other children burst into laughter, pointing at the dirt smudged through her hair. The girl looked a little embarrassed. She mumbled, as if to explain, "Miss, I just thought that flower I passed earlier... kind of looked like it was smiling!" "Flowers don't smile," the teacher said with a frown. "That shape doesn't follow the standard pattern or proportions." "But that's okay, Miss!" The girl pulled the same playful face as her flowerpot. "It doesn't have to be perfect!" "What I really made is..." "a moment of happiness turned into something that lasts!" Outside the window, Medowlyn found herself speaking the words at the very same time. So that was it. The little girl, and the garden, were both pieces of who she used to be. And that was it. It didn't have to be perfect, as long as the memory was a happy one.

The garden seemed to stretch on without end, while somewhere in the distance, a school bell rang.

Medowlyn dashed toward the only classroom in sight, whose windowsill loomed far above her, and, with a burst of effort, she leapt up and pulled herself onto it.

Through the window, she saw children sitting upright, completely absorbed in their craft lesson. And there, among their delicate, flawless creations, stood a little girl covered head to toe in dirt.

"Where did a kid that big come from?" voices chirped somewhere in the garden. Medowlyn opened her eyes. Towering above her were flowers, so tall they seemed to stretch far beyond her. The flowers here... could talk? She pushed herself to her feet and brushed the dirt from her dress. Thankfully, her coiffure was still intact. As her gaze wandered, she realized it wasn't just the flowers. Everything in the garden seemed to be watching her: a tiny clay pot, a single blade of grass, a little trowel, a clump of mud, even a patch of soil! They all stared with wide, curious eyes and wore friendly, if a little odd, expressions. They were far from perfect. Far from refined. Each of them was rough and earthy in its own way. And yet, Medowlyn felt a strange, familiar warmth. With a startled shriek, she turned and ran down the path.

She had no idea how much time had passed. It felt like floating on clouds... Like a single feather drifting inside a downy pillow.
At last, she landed on something soft — a cushion of floofalicious grass.

Everything was a mess. Medowlyn lunged for the troublemaking yarn balls, but they gave her no chance.
One after another, they rushed the window, bumping it open and bouncing out into the open air. In their wake, they carried off her delicate tools, combs, scissors, and curling irons, all swept away as they tumbled after them.

Medowlyn rushed to the window and leaned out. Beyond it stretched a sea of clouds, soft as a bed of cotton.
Without a second thought, she jumped.

The lady's maids finished curling the last of Medowlyn's hair.
Watching her from behind as she sat so still and intent, they quietly closed the door with a soft sigh. The girl had not slept for two days and nights, all for the sake of the ball.
Medowlyn didn't notice them leave. She was too caught up in her frustration — Once threaded through the beads, her hair would slip loose again, refusing to hold the full, petal-like curve she was trying to shape.
Nor did she notice the sound that had begun to fill the room, a soft gurgling, as if something were slowly rolling somewhere nearby.

At first, it was just a round, fuzzy little ball rolling past her in a blur.
Medowlyn paid it no mind. She figured it was just something her tired eyes had made up after staying awake too long.
But then came another. And another. More yarn balls skittered in by the second!

Before she could even react, they had spread to every corner of the room. They bumped and tumbled into one another with rolling sounds, throwing everything into disarray!

Medowlyn stood frozen. For a moment, she could not find a single word to describe what she was seeing.

The yarn balls, like mischievous little sprites, rolled about as they snatched up the delicate hair accessories scattered around the room, perching them on one another as makeshift hats and mustaches...
Before long, they had turned into a collection of lopsided little figures, crooked and absurd, adorned with hairpins, sporting tiny mustaches, and dressed up like grown-ups!
Everything was a mess!

The Coiffure Ball was the traditional coming-of-age ceremony of her kind, renowned for its exacting standards of perfection. From a young age, children were taught to tend to their hair with the utmost care. The strict grooming rituals required them to sit tall, move with grace, and maintain flawless composure at all times. The strands used to craft the commemorative hairwork were, as the old song went, smooth as silk and near divine: No trace of impurity, No sign of breakage, No hint of frizz, No weight of sorrow. As smooth as satin, As gentle as song. Thus it grows. Thus it is flawless. And Medowlyn was the finest among them — or rather, she was about to be.

Her worried pleas were met with one excuse after another, all about some "rules."
"It's not that I don't want to go. It's just... there's this new rule about a mandatory maintenance period after each trip..."
"We're, uh, getting things ready! Soon, we'll go get your master soon, just waiting for the um, procedures to go through..."

By the time Rebella finally managed to get a ride back to where she had said goodbye to her master, there was nothing left but dust in the wind.
And in that wind, an unclaimed sigh. Drifting, forever unheard.

"Have you heard? Did that girl really find the tri-colored gemstone her master kept going on about?!"
"No way! That's going to fetch a fortune..."

That morning, Gem Street was abuzz with news of the massive tri-colored gemstone Rebella had brought back. Merchants dealing in rare stones flocked to her doorstep, each offer higher than the last, only to be turned away every time.

By the second sunrise, a towering obelisk stood at the busiest intersection on Gem Street, commanding the gaze of all who passed. The tri-colored gemstone caught the light and scattered shifting prismatic colors across the ground.

"Stop!!!"
Every now and then, a cry like this would break the peace of Gem Street. Before long, a wave of chaos would ripple through the street, and everyone would know — the ever-rebellious girl had done it again.

"NO CLIMBING ON ROOFTOPS!"
"NO REBELLA ALLOWED!!!"

Warning signs sprang up along the street like mushrooms after a storm, only to be kicked apart just as quickly by the girl they were meant for.
"Rules, schmules! Not in my dictionary!"

There was a time when Rebella was someone entirely different. She wore exquisite gowns and lived in a grand manor beneath walls of ice and snow. She took pride in her family, in their abundance, their elegance, and in the measured, enigmatic way they spoke. Until the day came when the head of the family told her she would be sent to live with another "family," to trade her name for reputation, glory, and riches.
"You are too fragile. Think of this as your way of repaying us for all we have given you..."
That was when Rebella saw through the glitter of endless riches and gentle promises, and understood the price they truly demanded.

She tilted her head, then cast aside her corseted silk dress and climbed onto a passing supply truck.
To get lost without a destination... well, why not?

Her belly began chanting ceaselessly by the time she wandered to Chromawright Lane, a place famed for its gemstone craft. She was taken in by a kind-hearted but eccentric craftsman whose eyes shone like fluorite, just like hers.

Before long, she was scrambling up rooftops and leaping onto passing cars. Not a single corner of the street was spared her recklessness.

Her eyes, glinting with a blue-green shimmer in the night, were a gift she was born with. They set her apart, allowing her to spot hidden veins of ore faster than anyone else.

But the elder smiths told a very different story.
"Her eyes? Tsk... that's actually an impairment..."
"No one knows where she came from, and she's had no proper training. She won't last long."

Rumors drifted past Rebella's ears, only to be flicked away along with a casual scratch.
She paid no mind to the whispers of strangers. What she cared about were the colors of sunlight filtering through gemstones, the wind roaming freely across the rooftops, and the aroma rising from her master's cooking.
The smell of home.

Rebella soon realized that her master's humble gemstone workshop was the quietest place on the entire street. She sat on the rooftop, letting the wind pass her by, but couldn't figure it out. In the end, she hopped down.
"Master, what does family even mean?" Rebella asked.

The craftsman lifted his gaze from the polishing wheel and looked at Rebella, now seated beside him.
"Family, sweethearts, friends... all of them are essentially just labels and categories," he said. "Fragile, yet enduring. Sometimes, those labels give us a sense of security. But what truly matters is where you are, and what it is you really want."

Rebella seemed to catch hold of something unseen. "Then what do you want most?"
The man looked up toward a gap in the roof, where a strip of sky showed through.
"You know... there is a tri-colored gemstone mentioned in the old records, one that can bathe the land in dazzling hues at sunrise."
Wiping the sweat from his brow, her master spoke of a dream of a tri-colored gemstone.

Although the dream had nothing to do with Rebella, it piqued her curiosity nonetheless. From that day on, she began traveling with him, climbing mountains and crossing rivers in search of stones with strange and wondrous colors.

Out in the Starsea, Rebella sat atop a car once more, but this time, the direction was hers to choose.
Following her instincts and the strange colors only her eyes could catch, she pointed toward a path few had ever taken. She had thought of coming here before, but rumors of danger had always held her back.
The old craftsmen let her lead, giving her and her master free rein to explore, though they still had their doubts when Rebella stopped before an unremarkable cliff. However, as they skeptically broke through the rock and saw the gleam of a solid vein of rare ore within, they finally realized that Rebella had led them to a mountain-sized motherlode.

Everyone was thrilled, save Rebella. She kicked a small pebble along the ground, disappointed. It wasn't the tri-colored gemstone she had been searching for.
They called in more hands, and soon the air filled with the sound of chisels and hammers. Meanwhile, Rebella, tail swaying, drifted off into a bored nap.
By the time she woke, her companions had already driven off with their haul, leaving her behind.
Rebella patted her belly, then flopped onto the ground, spreading out into a big, soft pancake on the unfamiliar islet.
"I want meat," she said.

Her master smiled, his hair tousled like wild grass. He looked down at his pancaked apprentice and pointed toward a spot nearby. Rebella blinked. From within the broken cliff, something shimmered, strange colors catching the light...

The tri-colored gem was no dream. It was right there before her eyes.

"A fully intact tri-colored gemstone... refractive index... Hmm, hardness still needs testing..." "Master, I'm hungry... rawr." It was the third time her stomach had rumbled in protest. The moment her dream came true was also... the moment hunger caught up with her. And they had no vehicle for the return trip, nor food supplies.

As the stars shifted overhead, the urgency of survival began to outweigh her dreams. Rebella was grateful for her thick fur, and for the cold she had grown used to since childhood. She lay on the ground, talking with her master, who held the tri-colored gemstone with a contented smile. "Maybe a car will pass by any second now." "My dream right now is a pot of stew, just like the kind you used to make." "That's not a dream. That's a wish. A wish is something I can make happen. But a dream... is something out of reach, yet impossible to let go of." "So... the tri-colored gemstone is your dream, and now you've found it. But it doesn't seem—" "Look! A car!" Rebella, who had been sprawled on the ground, heard the sound of a passing vehicle. She got to her feet, clutching the tri-colored gemstone, and couldn't help but glance back. The wind had gone still. There was nothing there.

It all came back to her in that moment.
It had been like this once before. Left alone on a deserted Islet, starving and cold. The only difference was that back then, there had been no tricolored gem in her hands.
What she had instead was her master, hair tousled and smiling as ever.
She coaxed her onto the only open seat on a passing vehicle, telling her to find help once she was back on Gem Street. However, when Rebella returned and asked the smiths around for help, nobody cared to answer her call...

When the bidding had worn everyone thin, their eyes bloodshot as they pressed her to choose a buyer at last... Rebella rose to her feet, smiling, and brought the hammer down—

A crack raced down the fragile obelisk. The sharp sound rang out, piercing the stunned silence of the crowd. All that profit they held so dear shattered into a thousand iridescent fragments under the sun.
"There's your rules... in smithereens! Rawr~"

Amid the chaos, the angry screams, and the furious shouts, Rebella swiftly hitched a ride and sat on its roof. With the wind at her side, she set off on another journey into the unknown. She thought she heard a voice in the wind, laughter so familiar and warm, as if bidding her farewell.
But when she listened closely, there was nothing there after all...

But on Gem Street, no one believes in dreams. Beauty here is measured in wealth and status.
Then, one day, a few old craftsmen warmly invited Rebella and her master to join an expedition in search of new mineral sources. She said yes without asking a single question.

People stood in awe and snapped photos. Their quiet whispers quickly grew into open debates, because the rebellious girl who defied their wishes was sitting right in front of the obelisk. Rebella smirked at every person who approached with an offer, "More! This is the only copy, you know." The smiths scoffed. So much for her and that master of hers not caring about money! Just look at her, fishing for higher bids! Rebella didn't care for their mockery and focused on raising the price. She watched as the bidders stepped all over each other in the competition, and gemsmiths who worked together in the past traded barbs. The price didn't matter in that moment, nor did any "rules." The only thing that everyone cared about was who would profit in the end.

Isaki's eyes were glued to the TV screen, the ever-shifting light casting a pale glow across his face.
It was his favorite hero show, where the protagonists never gave up. No matter how many times the villains knocked them down, they always rose again and won in the end.
Isaki admired those heroes deeply, perhaps because that kind of "hero" was something someone like him, known to everyone as "Weakling Isaki," could never become.

"Pluck up the courage and give it a try." That was what the grown-ups always told Isaki.
But the thing was... little Isaki had no idea how anyone was supposed to "pluck up" courage.

Walking down the street, he might flinch at a bird suddenly fluttering past. Sitting in the shade, he'd startle when a fruit dropped from above.
...
Things like that happened all the time.

Isaki's five older siblings had already found their place in the things they loved. As the youngest, he was allowed to be a late bloomer, and the grown-ups were patient with his timid nature. He could do nothing, stay tucked away at home, and simply wait each day for his favorite hero show to come on.
Would it really matter if "Weakling Isaki" lived an unremarkable, aimless life? After all, wasn't it enough to have the heroes on TV to keep him company?

"Hello...?"
It was a strange, wondrous moment. For the first time in his life, Isaki found himself greeting someone else first. Where had that courage come from?

The kabuto beetle took a step forward.
Isaki had never been this close to a "stranger" before. His body was ready to tremble, but he tried his best. Quietly clenching his fists, he managed to steady himself.
Then the beetle took another step. Now they were only inches apart.
Isaki gathered every bit of courage he had and slowly reached out with a small, hesitant finger. In that instant, his fingertip met the beetle's horn.

Feeling its quiet intent, Isaki smiled.
"Nice to meet you... friend!"

Is this... really enough? The moment the familiar ending theme of the hero show began to play, the certainty in Isaki's heart suddenly shifted into a question. Was it because the lyrics just happened to sing, "No weakling stays that way for long. Even a lowly bug can grow strong. With a heart that defies and a spirit so true, the hero's path is calling to you"? Isaki wasn't quite sure.

BOOM—
Thunder and lightning raged outside.

"Weakling Isaki" buried himself beneath the heavy blanket, trying to shut out the world and steady his trembling body.
BOOM — another violent thunderclap shook the room, his safe haven, to its core.
The items on his shelves and hooks rattled loose, tumbling down onto his shaking body.
get_storytitle: The Weakling Hero and His Friend

get_text: Mmph... Could this be... the end of the world?! Isaki could only let out a frightened whimper. Then, all at once, everything fell silent. Maybe... the world didn't end after all? Realizing this, Isaki found a tiny spark of courage he rarely felt, and he slowly peeked out from beneath the blanket. That's when he saw it. A kabuto beetle stood before him, head held high. The enormous moon filled the window behind it, casting the beetle in a silhouette that looked just like a hero's dramatic entrance from a TV show. Did it... protect me?

"Heh, Heh... Wounded like that, and you still think you can stop me?"
"Evil is about to rule the world. Give up, you weakling."
"...Hmph."
"Oh? Still resisting, even now?"

"If you insist... then I'll show you how a weakling becomes a hero!"

"Th-This... this is my new friend, Daikabutomaru! C-Can I keep it?"

The grown-ups were, of course, delighted to see Isaki make a new friend, and even more so to see him beginning to change. But, as every TV show goes, that's exactly when a bit of trouble is bound to show up.
"That kabuto beetle... isn't it the one raised by that 'legendary' beetle trainer in the neighborhood?"
"Shouldn't we check with its owner first?"

For timid Isaki, dealing with strangers was another challenge altogether. But with Daikabutomaru by his side, he seemed to have found a kind of courage he had never known before.
Following the address the grown-ups had given him, he pattered all the way to the beetle trainer's house and, without a second thought, rang the doorbell. The old "Weakling Isaki" would never have had the courage to do that.

The "legendary" beetle trainer opened the door and gave Isaki and Daikabutomaru a flat look.
"If you want it, then keep it. I can't take in too many weaklings anyway..."
"...Huh?"
Isaki froze.
Of course. To a trainer like him, only the strongest beetles that kept winning mattered. He didn't need weaklings, and he had never cared that Daikabutomaru had gone missing in the first place.

"Mmmrrghhh..."
The sound that forced its way out of Isaki's throat was deeper than anything he had ever made before.
"You. Listen up!"
"Daikabutomaru is not a weakling! I'll train it to become the strongest fighting beetle... and defeat you!"

"Come on, Daikabutomaru! Time for strength training!"
"Next up, endurance!"
"Watch closely and dodge my mattock swing! You can do it, Daikabutomaru!"
"I'm running faster now, so you've got to fly even faster!"

Training alongside Daikabutomaru, Isaki was changing. He was taking on the very things he once feared, pushing himself further each time. And more often than not, he surpassed what the grown-ups thought he could do.

As Daikabutomaru fought to overcome its weaknesses, Isaki was doing the same.

"Weakling." That was what people called those who were too afraid to face challenges, too afraid to change.
That was who Isaki used to be: a "weakling" who hid away in his room, content to do nothing but watch his favorite hero shows, never taking a single step toward anything different.
get_storytitle: The Weakling Hero and the Challenge

get_text: "Beetle battle... begin!" "Go! Daikabutomaru!" There was no need to fear. No need to panic. No need to run. Not even for a single moment did the thought of "what if we lose" cross Isaki's mind. We're going to win. No doubt. "And the winner of the beetle battle is..." "Isaki and Daikabutomaru!"

"Congratulations. You won."
Isaki froze for a moment. The "legendary" beetle trainer, despite losing the match, was actually reaching out to him with a friendly hand.

"But... didn't you look down on Daikabutomaru for being a 'weakling'?"
"Haha, not at all. Every bug is a cherished comrade to me. But beetle battles carry a real risk of injury, and that risk is even greater for 'weaklings.' That's something I never want to see... So when I judge one to be too fragile, I usually let it return to the wild."

"But this time... I was wrong."
The beetle trainer, who had always seemed stern and rigid, suddenly broke into a smile. He crouched down and placed a hand on Isaki's head, gently ruffling his hair.
"You and Daikabutomaru are both remarkable. You're heroes."

Isaki had never imagined that one day, he would hear words like that.
"So? What do you say? Ready to take the next step... and win the real beetle championship?"

Something lit up in his eyes. It could only be called hope. He fell silent for a moment, then gave a firm, determined nod.
"Yes! I can do it! Deeeefinitely!"

"No weakling stays that way for long. Even a lowly bug can grow strong. With a heart that defies and a spirit so true, the hero's path is calling to you."
After their intense training, Isaki, still catching his breath, murmured the line to Daikabutomaru resting atop his head.

"It's... my favorite line." Isaki lifted his gaze to the endless blue sky.

"I didn't really understand it before. But now I — no, we, we've actually made it, Daikabutomaru."
"Come on. Let's go challenge the world!"

The next day at school, Yunguo's group turned in a yellowing tomato seedling.
"Didn't you all want to be in her group before?"
"Hah, what kind of 'prodigy' is that?"

Blushing, yet with a hopeful spark in her eyes, Yunguo said, "W-We didn't get the result wrong... it was the process. Next time, we can fix it together."
No one replied, but that was all right.

By the time Yunguo brought the tomato seedling home, hidden under her clothes, it was already past dinner.
At this hour, Granny would usually be chatting away in someone else's courtyard, so there was no chance of running into her—

"What are you sneaking in there?" Granny caught her red-handed, her gaze landing right on the yellowing seedling.
"You're not planning to swap this out for one you grew yourself and turn that in, are you?"

Yunguo's face flushed deep red. She couldn't say a word. She just closed her eyes and braced herself for the storm...

But Granny only gave her head a gentle pat and sighed. "Not every seedling will grow strong just because you tend it with care. There are storms, droughts, pests... all kinds of hardship. You never know what they'll come up against. You have to face that. So do they."

Day 193 since leaving Granny's place. Yunguo sat by the riverbank, her chin resting in her hands. She thought about the last packet of seeds she had planted. They should be blooming by now. Maybe there would be fruit soon... It was a shame she wouldn't get to see it. The Islet where she had planted those seeds was nowhere to be found. People always leave. She vaguely understood that. Yunguo let out a long sigh and counted the Dough and produce in her bag, trying to stay hopeful. If she didn't eat or drink, she could last another five days. Still... it was so cold. She hugged her knees and buried her face in her arms, rubbing her eyes. Suddenly, everything went dark. But she felt warm, as if she were buried in soft soil. It almost felt nice, like she could just fall asleep like that. Then she heard the wind. She heard water flowing. She heard insects chirping. She saw an earthworm wriggling beside her, loosening the soil... Wait, where did that earthworm come from?!

Yunguo woke up, still a little dazed from the nap. The river before her shimmered with the hues of the setting sun. Beside her, the phone lit up with a message from Granny: "What did you eat today?"

Almost without thinking, Yunguo typed, "Nothing yet," but her finger hovered above the send button. After a moment, she deleted it and started over: "Gonna make some congee with apples tonight. Should be yummy."

Yunguo pulled up a number from her contacts. Granny had once said it belonged to a proper grown-up who'd traveled the universe all alone. "If you ever get stuck, you go ask him."
"H-Hello... I'm Yunguo, from Mount Zhuxi. We met when I was little... I've... um... I've been livin' by myself for half a year now, and I've kinda run out of money..."

She practiced saying it aloud, but the more she thought about it, the more it felt wrong, like she was calling just to be a trouble.
"...This is my first time leavin' Granny... I came out on my own to learn how to grow things... She asked me to visit you first, and maybe get some lil' advice about livin' on my own."

After practicing over and over until she was sure she could say it smoothly, Yunguo took a deep breath and dialed the number. To her surprise, it was answered after just one ring.
"H-Hello! Mr. Mobai..."
"Huh? I'm not Mobai. This is Elsa..."

"S-Sorry!!!"
Yunguo hung up in a panic, her face turning bright red even though there was no one else around on the unfamiliar islet.
A moment later, her phone rang again. The caller ID showed "Mr. Mobai."

"What's it like outside? Is it this dark too?"
Yunguo heard her own voice, as if asking someone.
"No, it's bright out there. Let me loosen the soil a bit so you can get through."
The earthworm spoke as it wriggled upward, working so hard that Yunguo was moved. But earthworms can't talk, can they? They shouldn't be able to!
"What if it's too cold outside?"
She heard herself ask again, glancing around at the warm, dark soil that surrounded her.
"There's sunlight! Once you find the sun, it won't be cold anymore."
The earthworm happily burrowed its way out, and a beam of light broke through the soil into Yunguo's eyes, almost blinding, but warm.

At the foot of Mount Zhuxi, along the ridges of the rice paddies, bamboo flasks and woven baskets dotted the path. The villagers, bent over the fields since dawn, were just settling down for a well-earned cup of tea.
A joke went around that while everyone else's baskets held crops or tools, the Yuns' carried their two-year-old granddaughter, Blushberry.

Unlike the other grey-furred toddlers, this little one looked as if a fluffy sun had tumbled into the bamboo grove — red, radiant, and bright as a ripe fruit on harvest day. A pity, though. No matter what anyone tried, she never smiled. The moment a stranger came near, she'd shrink away. And on bad days, she'd burst into loud, panicked wails.

"Nobles who obtained the seed sought to prove their power and prestige. Artists who found it wished to display their refinement and taste. Wealthy merchants who got their hands on it longed to flaunt their riches before the world.
Each planted it with care, treating it like gold, yet none waited long enough to see it sprout. Tired of waiting, they called it filthy and foul, ugly and useless, and cast it aside.
Then a farmer found the seed. To him, it was simply a seed, planted alongside his other crops. Before long, it sprouted and bloomed, bright red like the sun.
The farmer went about his daily work in the fields, pausing now and then to admire its petals and leaves, offering a smile as he carried away its scent. That fragrance, once it brushed against anyone who came near, would linger with them forever."

They continued to stare at each other in confusion. Yunguo tilted her head and blinked.
"Granny... I don't quite understand."

Granny stood up, brushed the dirt from her clothes, then helped the bewildered Yunguo to her feet and patted the soil from her skirt.
"My little Blushberry," she said, "you're that seed, growing slowly, soaking up the scent of earth and grass, waiting for your day to bloom."

Yunguo's fuzzy ears twitched, and a glimmer of hope sparked in her eyes.
Granny let out a quiet sigh of relief, thinking the child had finally come around...

"Could my Blushberry be from that seed?"
Grandmother and granddaughter exchanged a puzzled look. Granny cleared her throat and began a story.

"Once upon a time, there was a seed as round as a rice dumpling. Anyone who laid eyes on it fell in love instantly. They said it would grow into the most beautiful, one-of-a-kind flower in the world... but no one had ever seen it bloom."

It was the tail end of another winter break. In the southern chill, Yunguo was hoping for snow. If the mountain got snowed in, she wouldn't have to go back to kindergarten. "Schoolbag's mended. Hm? The water bottle's cracked? Better pick a sturdier one this time..." Yunguo crouched beside Granny in the little vegetable patch by their front door, poking at the soil with her tiny spade. She kept glancing up at the sky while Granny talked on about all the things she would need for school. Suddenly, she spoke up. "Granny, do I look strange? Do I smell weird?" Granny's hands paused as she loosened the soil. She leaned close to Yunguo's little head and gave a careful sniff all around before answering seriously. "Yes, you do." Hearing Granny's answer, Yunguo thought, I really am no good...

In the rice paddies, a mound of green Archiboos suddenly scattered, revealing a giggling girl, caked in mud and clutching an armful of giant fruits and vegetables.

"That can't be Blushberry, can it? Blushberry never smiles. She only knows how to cry at strangers."
But who else could it be? Red as ripe fruit, like a little sun fallen into the bamboo grove.

The tale spread like wildfire, from one mouth to ten, ten to a hundred, until it became local legend: That day, little Yunguo grew herself a heart, right there in the rice paddies.
A miracle, plain and simple.

Mount Zhuxi was in an uproar. The chestnut vendor hollered it mid-stir to his customer. The postman, cooling off in the shade, passed it to the sugar painting artist. The repairman patching a bike tire called it out to the passing peddler— "The Yuns' kid is missing!" Did it matter whether anyone actually knew who the Yuns were? Not a bit. Just spread the word. Nothing could go wrong if everyone helped look. Blushberry — that was the kid who never smiled, the one who burst into tears the moment she saw a stranger. Granny was by the well in front of the bamboo house, washing mugwort leaves when she caught wind of it. She always boiled them in summer for the little one's bath, to keep the mosquitoes away and keep the rash at bay... Wait, who did you say was missin'? "Told you, her Gramps's no good at mindin' kids." Grabbing her palm fan, she charged down the mountain. The search party for Blushberry stirred the entire mountain. By the time the sun was about to set, everyone finally let out a breath of relief.

So lately, her grandparents had been carrying her around in a bamboo basket, hoping she'd get used to being around people — some kind of training or exposure or whatever they call it. But little Blushberry had never budged from the depths of her basket. The Skies Above as their witness, all anyone had seen were two fuzzy ears poking out. Now, the basket had gone quiet. Perhaps she was asleep. They decided to sneak a peek. It was empty. Empty?!

"Whose old tale did you pick up this time?" Yunguo asked, tilting her head with a squinty smile.
Granny was caught red-handed. A faint blush crept across her cheeks. She gave Yunguo's head a firm but playful tap, muttering under her breath as she took the girl's hand to lead her home.

Yunguo squeezed back, tilting her face to the sky and sticking out her tongue to taste the air. Suddenly, she reached up, as if trying to catch something.
"Granny, the snow's coming. Can I be that farmer?"

During the ceremonial wrestling match held to honor their deity, Dorjelang sat by the lakeside and watched the spectacle of fervor and power. Out of place and even slightly dissonant with the scene was the low, chanted verses from the herder next to him: When chaos gave birth to earth and sky, White yak from the lotus did arise, With ears that hear all earthly things, Nose that scents far and wide, Wings to soar o'er mountains and rivers, Hooves to race across plains and fissures, He is the mighty mountain high, He is the gentle flowing stream, He is the father working hard, He is the mother's loving heart, He tames the strong and lifts the meek, His righteous name through ages speak, His legend in our hearts engraved, Through song we sing his ageless praise. The song spoke of the highland deity. Legend has it that "he" looked just like everyone else in the tribe, with long flowing hair, a strong athletic build, and mighty long horns, and that "he" danced to the heavens and sang for the earth. "Behold, it brings success. Behold, it's filled with fortune. And behold, it possesses the eternal..." Dorjelang caught himself humming along. He glanced at his own reflection in the emerald lake... Me? I look nothing like the deity, moo. A buddy from a neighboring tribe came over. Dorjelang could see his messy hair and his beautiful, sturdy horns that put his own feeble ones to shame. His buddy stroked his chin in deep thought.

This was Dorjelang's sixteenth year living on the highland pastures.
Back then, he knew nothing of the world beyond.

Dorjelang was seen as someone who needed protection in his tribe. He thought if he could be a little stronger and a little tougher, put on a stern face and look a little fiercer... then maybe he would actually become more capable.
Perhaps due to his frailty, there were many things off-limits to him, like going down to the river, wrestling, or herding alone. Concerned gazes followed him around whenever he tried to get involved.
The old herder who tutored him said that his body wasn't as strong because he carried all the good fortune of the highlands on his head, that he was a child blessed by their deity.
Whenever they took him out to herd, the wolves would scatter, snowstorms would cease, and blood-sucking insects would disperse.

Dorjelang wanted to believe in it.
get_storytitle: Over the Mountain Far From Home

get_text:
When he woke from the dream, the moonlit figure was gone, and next to him, there was only the foxtail hat.
His companion had kept watch under the moon, coming and departing in soft silence. No mountains or rivers, nor winds of the highlands could ever scatter the memories of its devoted silhouette.
Though years may pass, its form remains, timeless beneath the moonlight's glow.
Though the permafrost before dawn may never melt, the warmth in his heart endures.

It was the thirty-ninth day of Dorjelang's arduous journey across the endless mountains.
He stood at a station in the Starsea and glanced back at the dawn-gilded peaks of his homeland. He tucked the little foxtail hat into his luggage and moved on.
The boy, once sheltered by so many, had finally made it over the mountains.

Deep in the night by a stream, Dorjelang rested his head on his luggage and watched as Doggie snored beside him. He hadn't noticed the whites in its fur before, realizing just how old it had grown. It's only minor injuries, we'll heal soon. He told himself as he fell asleep. Wolf howls came to Dorjelang's dreams, and he tried opening his eyes. Unsure if they were actually opened, Dorjelang believed he saw Doggie on a moonlit hill with head raised to the sky. Its graying fur seemed to glow as it let out the longest unfettered cry in its life, and the woods answered with an echoing chorus of wolfsong.

Unable to convince Doggie to leave, Dorjelang could only watch as it busied itself with scouting the path ahead, lagging behind, catching up again, and panting breathlessly with stalks of foxtail in its mouth, and even a rabbit... Wait, drop that right now! Strange, this was supposed to be a journey that took them farther and farther away from home, but with Doggie's company, every day, he felt blessed with luck like all the days before. Still, danger and uncertainty drew ever closer, and when he picked up the dull cracking sounds echoing through the quiet mountains, he knew an avalanche was coming. By the time he woke up between a slush of mud and snow, he had no idea how long he'd been buried. A wet tongue licked his eyes, blurring the moon in his vision, and under it, he saw Doggie whimpering and digging through the snow. So the deity has blessed me after all! he thought and smiled, not daring to make a sound for fear of stirring the mountain again. Doggie had suffered a broken hind leg and a gash on its scalp. Dorjelang applied some medicinal herbs to the wound and grabbed some foxtail to weave a little hat, so as to keep Doggie from scratching its head. Holding his companion, Dorjelang thought about turning back to their village, but the way back was even longer than continuing forward. Doggie barked furiously in protest, as if to say, "All my work would have been for nothing if you turned back now." Man and dog then traveled even farther.

As time passed, Dorjelang grew up to be the weakest in the tribe, while Doggie became the alpha of the canines. However, the herders had always suspected that Doggie was actually a grassland wolf.

Whenever Doggie tried to howl, Dorjelang would gently hold his muzzle shut, worried that he might leave with a wolf pack that picked up the call.

Doggie's name was simply Doggie. He stayed by Dorjelang's side through everything like a faithful guardian — herding with him, wrestling with him, accompanying him on pilgrimages to mountain tops...
Even now, he wanted to keep Dorjelang company on his journey away from home.

It was the ninth day of Dorjelang's arduous journey across the endless mountains.
He had prepared himself for the inevitable solitude that came with leaving home, but as he woke from a dream, he found a figure basking under the moon.

Doggie, his childhood companion, had secretly followed him. He was grinning and lolling his tongue, as if to say, "Took you long enough to notice me."

The old herders used to tell the story of how a flood once swept little Dorjelang out of the shed where he'd been sunbathing. When they finally found him, Doggie was whimpering, and Dorjelang was crying even louder.

The two little ones had just opened their eyes and were wrestling each other under an ownerless hat. Everyone thought they'd go their separate ways, but some bonds, once formed, could only deepen.

Frightened by their fear, Dorjelang fled in panic, accidentally bumping into something as he ran...
Amidst the rising dust, dizzy and disoriented, Dorjelang saw a massive figure approaching. He could barely contain his excitement at the prospect of meeting someone like himself.

The dust settled, but Dorjelang didn't see anyone.
"Tsk! Tsk tsk! Who?! Who broke down the walls of my workshop?..."
Dorjelang looked down and saw a little one wearing a white feather scarf. She looked up at him judgingly.
"You again?"

This place probably isn't right for him... Dorjelang scratched his head nervously and shook it. No, it wasn't about fitting in. He left home to find his buddy and bring him back.

Dorjelang looked at the stage again as another group of laughing performers took their turn. This was the world of dreams and aspirations that his buddy lived in. Would he even want to return with him at all?

Lost in thought, Dorjelang found himself drawn closer to the stage. The mesmerizing lights kept shifting, and no one noticed when one of the light poles started to wobble.
He instinctively caught the falling pole, but when he turned around, he saw countless fearful, confused eyes staring at him, as if trying to see right through his otherness.

In this world, he could easily destroy everything with a slight movement of his hand.
His turquoise beads, horned barbaric hat, towering build, and thunderous voice... everything about him struck fear in others.
He realized then that being powerful and mighty wasn't something to be proud of after all.

The first among them to think of leaving was his buddy. Pulling Dorjelang along, he made grand plans of how he would conquer the endless mountains and see the world beyond in pursuit of his dreams. Dreams? What are... dreams? Buddies stick together till the end, so you're coming too, Dorjelang. Dorjelang was worried that he'd hold his buddy back, being as frail as he was. But his friend had unwavering faith in him. Before they left, his buddy got caught "loaning" a couple of barley buns from an old herder. Dorjelang went for the rescue, but froze at the doorway. "HAHMM? You have no right to keep him on the pastures forever..." On the glimmering highlands where heaven is just a few steps away, too many struggle to make the journey because of a weighted heart. "You've never believed in him. You just think he's weak, and needs protection..." Outside the house, Dorjelang listened as Doggie came over. As always, it sat beside him, panting with a lolling tongue, as if saying, "Eavesdropping too, huh?" "How long will you deceive him with these words? Are you going to keep sheltering him his whole life?" Dorjelang gazed up at the sunset's glow, at the deity watching over the highlands. "There is no divine blessing. He has the same horns and fur on his head as us, plus a yak horn hat that I traded with barley buns..." Please let all my good fortune rest upon my buddy's head— "I have my own dreams and my own path to follow, so I won't stay... but save half the barley bun for him. I'm leaving this place..." May he be safe, free, and prosperous on the journey of his dreams. This was Dorjelang's sixteenth year living on the highland pastures. In the empty house his buddy left behind, the old herder threw him a bundle of supplies, his mustache bristling with anger. He told Dorjelang to get out there and bring back his good-for-nothing buddy. Finally, he understood there was a kind of longing in this world that words cannot capture. He wanted to cross this mountain, and the next one beyond, and countless more after.

It was Dorjelang's first day at the Galactic Bazaar. All his life, he had felt adrift in a vast sea of people — without direction, without a place to belong. After hauling five boxes of goods for a shopkeeper at the street corner, it suddenly occurred to him that everyone here was so small, and he was incredibly strong in comparison... Maybe... I can actually help them? The revelation filled him with unprecedented joy and the urge to act, but he must stay calm. A slight turn of his body was enough to send someone flying... Mmmooo? Wasn't someone here just now? After eight victims, six cracked chairs, four shattered steps, and three flattened billboards, all eyes were trained on him with terror. He spent all his money making amends, then hurried through every intersection, anxiously avoiding anyone who came too close. Finally, he found a quiet corner to settle in. Crouching down, he took a deep breath and reminded himself to exercise more self-restraint. When he lifted his head again, he realized he was at a high point in the bazaar. Following the sound of music, he saw cheerful crowds, lively stages, and a shimmering magician's tent below...

Dorjelang had once been small and fragile, the kind who stayed tucked behind others, always in need of protection. But everyone in the workshop had seen him, without meaning to, snap table legs, crush teacups, and crack plates... so they could only assume the gentle giant had been far too modest about his strength. To Dorjelang, being able to use that strength to help those weaker than himself was a kind of luck he held dear. It had nothing to do with meeting anyone's expectations. It simply meant that when he wanted to help, he could. Master Mufflin, however, insisted he had yet to understand. She watched him as he left and remembered how her bright-eyed student dug her out of a pile of magazines in the basement five years ago... No, scratch that part. She had been standing atop that very pile, arms folded, quizzing him on hats, while he answered every question with ease. Learning on his own, in secret? How dare he?! In her irritation, she leapt down and twisted her ankle... No, scratch that part too. By the magazine pile, Dorjelang had been weaving with reeds, recreating every hat on those pages. The audacity to learn in secret... She turned away with a scowl. Even so, Dorjelang had earned approval with a "Be here at eight tomorrow morning." For him, it brought a different kind of joy and anticipation, something he didn't feel when helping others. Five years had passed since Dorjelang became a hat-making apprentice. On this day, he chose a dandelion to adorn the hat meant to welcome spring. With his new kit slung over his back, he set out once more. He still dreamed of the past — of jagged mountain paths strewn with stone, of snow and forests, of winds that never ceased, and of foxtail grass swaying gently in their wake. The dandelion lifted in the breeze and drifted toward distant mountains, as if gathering those dreams. He wondered who it would stir awake this time.

Unable to bear it any longer, Mufflin hopped down from the parapet in frustration.
On the ground, she stood a full five heads shorter than him, yet her sharp, rapid-fire scolding gave her an almost towering presence. She launched into a tirade, rattling off every misstep of his apprenticeship, from the six times he had smashed into walls over the past five years to the overly neat pile of yarn from the night before.

"You're a hatmaker! Stop wasting your time on trivial things, and go think about why we make hats!"

Dorjelang scratched his head sheepishly and nodded, which only irritated his master further, her white feather scarf slipping askew.

Shortly after, Dorjelang sat obediently by the rooftop grill, his limbs tucked in. Across from him, Master Mufflin stood with her arms crossed, glaring down at her student.
"How long have you been my student?" she demanded. But before he could answer, she jabbed a finger at his nose. "Five years! It's about time you graduated!"

Dorjelang didn't respond. His expression stayed grave as he sank into thought, and, as always, an awkward silence stretched between them.

Just as he finished, a passing senior, buried beneath a stack of fresh fabric, casually hollered for Dorjelang to help carry the load. The cook followed, smiling as she hooked two buckets of sweet soup onto his arms for a quick delivery to the canteen. Dorjelang nodded solemnly at every request, yet a glint in his eyes betrayed a secret pride. It was clear he relished the weight of such responsibilities. Up on the rooftop, Master Mufflin was snacking on roasted silkworm cocoons. Watching the big oaf dash back and forth across the yard, she clicked her tongue in irritation and stripped the skewer clean in one bite. Flick. The skewer shot forward and struck Dorjelang squarely in the back before bouncing away. He scratched the spot in confusion, then tilted his head up toward the rooftop.

This was Dorjelang's fifth year as a hat-making apprentice.
By the window, he studied the two fabric flowers in his hands with quiet intensity, weighing which one would better suit a hat meant to welcome the spring.

Suddenly, a cry for help rang out from a senior apprentice in the courtyard. A harsh gust of wind had swept the drying materials into a chaotic, tumbling flurry. With a thunderous rumble of footsteps, Dorjelang charged out. But the camera faithfully captured everything in sight, including a greenhorn who accidentally tore a hole in the tent just as another wave of yellow sand came with a gust of wind.

"And it sounds so... cold."
"The seawater IS cold!"

Orange like the sun, yet not as vast or as daunting. She thought with relief that maybe the stars, of all things, were just the right warmth. "Those are human torches." Her companion said and turned away. The soft hem of their garment swayed in the water, and the waves in the wake of their departure bobbed Nerina up and down. Her companion had already left the grove, leaving only a trail of bubbles behind. The bubbles carried a message, urging her on: "Hurry. You'll be late for class." A coral pointer struck her lyre, breaking her out of her reverie. Sometimes pausing for a second, other times much longer, long enough for a tiny planula to mature into a massive coral. Only after such an agonizingly long wait would the next note of the section slowly emerge. This was the same section where Nerina almost passed out from holding her breath during the previous rehearsal. And when the next note finally came, she nearly drowned herself again with deep, desperate inhales. She refused to move her hand again, because she couldn't fathom the meaning behind the piece. Maybe it was about an old sea turtle taking a stroll, or even the lives of seahorses, who were often motionless between the corals. In any case, it certainly wasn't a hymn that praised and celebrated the gift of joy from the Ocean God, as her teacher had claimed.

The soft sound of currents breaking into tiny bubbles filled the space around her, and Nerina knew she was no longer alone in the coral grove.
