"There's always a way to stay, as long as you want to stay," the girl said. "That's how it goes."

"So you want to stay, but you're too light. The wind would carry you away." The girl with pigtails nodded.
Nerina breathed a sigh of relief. The explanations were long and complicated, and as she explained, the girl kept adding even more questions, leaving her flustered and spinning in circles.
"Then just... make yourself heavier."

"Why aren't you answering me?"
"I... don't know either."
"What do you mean you don't know?!" The drooped pigtails sprang back up. "You don't have a destination? No plan?"
"When the wind comes, I'll go. I can't stop."

Nerina had no way to hide from the "currents" on land. When the wind comes, she'd be lifted into the clouds. And when the wind stops, she'd drift slowly back down.
But the girl couldn't understand. She leaned in close, warmth radiating from her as she blinked with curious eyes, "What do you mean?"

"Wait, you mean... you're leaving?!"
The girl with pigtails clutched Nerina's arm, her hair standing on end. "Where are you going? When are you planning to leave? How? We've only just become friends! Do you really have to go so soon? Are you going home? I don't even know where you live..."

The questions came rapid-fire, one after another, and Nerina felt like she was back underwater again — tiny bubbles bursting all around her, sounds layering and overlapping until her little head was overwhelmed.

Beneath the brilliant sunset, on the soft golden sands, a cheerful melody from a lyre can be heard.
"Boop~ Bloop-boop~ boop-bloop, boop~"
A little girl with pigtails danced to the tune. When the song ended, her hair bounced with the applause.

"What's this song about?"
"Maria and I making pottery, picking olives, and eating grapes together."
"Ooh~ It must all happened on a beautiful sunny day, right?"
"...Bloop."
"That sounds wonderful! What about ours? If you wrote a song about me fixing your lyre today, what would it sound like?"

Nerina didn't need long to think. The strings vibrated once more, and the melody came. Opening with a light and gleeful tune for the serendipitous discovery of seashells, the melody softened into careful, bouncing notes that told the delicate work of the girl's repair on the lyre, before finally slowing into a bittersweet goodbye.

The hermit crab poked its head out of the shell and, realizing it was wobbling around in someone's pocket, quietly retreated back inside. Nerina stood in a daze. There's always a way to stay, as long as I want to stay. Last time, she wanted to leave, so she set off and came to land. But this time, she wanted to stay, so she clutched the shells in her hand tightly and readied herself for a second "departure."
"Mama, look! The fishies are swimming over!"

That day, the Starsea was as clogged up as Monday mornings during rush hour. The senior patrol officers all exchanged knowing glances in the break room, their eyes full of unspoken implications.
"Hey, rookie—" The captain pointed to the new face in the corner.

The other patrol officers began whispering among themselves.
"That one couldn't even find her way two hundred meters outside the rest area last month."
"Oy, can't have them say that we're picking on a girl now."
"Right, then you get out there."
"Nope!"
"Alright rookie, consider this your orientation. You're up." The captain made his decision.

"Enough with the theatrics," A cold voice cut in. "You look more like a monkey swinging between branches."
Eyes watched as Harpeno's patrol bike eclipsed the sky like a chromatic cloud of divine punishment, hot on the wheels of the speeding ball of flame.

The drunk driver laughed amidst the flames and slammed the throttle to the floor. The two vehicles then became tangled trails of light on a chase across the Starsea. The rulebreaker thought he had the upper hand until he realized Harpeno was intentionally driving him toward a dust lane in the Starsea, a place where even signals couldn't escape.

This was Harpeno's first time handling rush hour on her own. Three cargo trucks created a complete gridlock at the intersection while fighting for the right of way, and a long line of angry, honking vehicles stretched behind them. A few drivers leaned against their doors, pontificating about the day's big Starsea news, and couldn't care less when they saw Harpeno's patrol car approaching.

"Little lady, get your supervisor," a stubbly-faced truck driver waved dismissively at her. "This isn't the place to play house."
Harpeno was silent. Her boot heels clicked against the pavement as she walked straight between the three deadlocked trucks.
"First truck." She pointed at the stubbly-faced driver's vehicle. "Your transport permit expired three months ago."
She turned to the next two trucks and continued, "Second truck, you're overloaded. Third truck, your right rear brake light is out."
She swiftly wrote out three tickets to follow.
"Now," she looked up. "Do I need to teach you gentlemen how to reverse, too?"
The three drivers' expressions immediately changed.
"Do you have any idea what we're hauling? You think you can afford to pay for the delay?"
"I certainly can't, but I can make you pay a whole lot more." She waved her ticket book. "Want to try me?"

Just then, an ambulance siren began to wail in the distance, but it wasn't getting any closer — it was stuck at the very back of the queue.
"Everyone, clear the way!" Harpeno suddenly raised her voice. She jumped onto the roof of the nearest vehicle and held up her megaphone and body camera. "Listen up, everyone! Left three lanes move forward in order, right two lanes stay put. Blue cargo truck, move two car lengths to the right — yes, you! Anyone who refuses to follow instructions can kiss their license goodbye!"
Her commands were clear, assertive, and indisputable.

The drivers who'd been onlookers up until now instinctively obeyed her words. When someone tried to cut in line, a single icy glare from Harpeno was enough to discourage their attempt and put them back in their place.
Gradually, the hopeless knot of traffic began to loosen. When the ambulance finally passed through, the drivers spontaneously honked their horns — the way Starsea drivers give thanks.
"Nice work, Miss 'Tyrant'!"
Nobody knew who started it, but everyone agreed that the nickname was a perfect fit for their decisive, no-nonsense new patrol officer.

The captain was waiting for Harpeno by the door after the team wrapped up debriefing.
"You've become the talk of all Starsea drivers after your battle today." He said.
"Hungry."
"Come again?" The captain had to clean out his ear. He could've sworn he just heard Harpeno meow like a cat.
"Are we getting barbecue or hot pot?" Harpeno flopped onto the lounge chair, seemingly drained. "Energy level critical."
Soft laughter rang out behind her as the senior officers exchanged new looks with each other. This time, feeling much closer to their new colleague.

In her new uniform, neatly pressed and rigid as the iron clauses of the law, Harpeno began her probationary patrol under Instructor Chen.

Cargo truck "No. 50" lay wheezing on the roadside greenery, puffing white smoke and barely hanging on. Its driver, Lee, rubbed his hands nervously and explained, "It's nothing, just a minor malfunction..."
Harpeno's detector began blaring.

Everyone in the Starsea calls her the "Tyrant."
Harpeno loves the nickname. Her patrol bike is the needle that passes between Starsea routes and stitches unruly vehicles back into the traffic network of order.

One day, some young aristocrat with a souped-up ride painted with flame decals smashed through a parking sign at the Galactic Bazaar. "I am the WIND! No one can catch the WIND!" He hollered. His drunken laughter was insufferably pompous as he sped away, and every public LED screen across the Starsea lit up to cover this chaotic spectacle.

She examined and read out the data, "Your actual mileage exceeded the allowed maximum by 40%, and the engine is severely deteriorated. You're lucky that it hasn't led to graver consequences." She looked toward the cargo hold, where countless puppies, kittens, along with a few long-haired rabbits and call ducks, scattered haphazardly among the shipment. The long journey had already left several of them looking queasy, but to Harpeno's surprise, the temperature inside the was quite comfortable, and the space was clean with hardly any odor.
"They're all strays I picked up along the way. If I'd left them outside in this weather, they probably wouldn't make it..." Lee's voice grew quieter and quieter.

Harpeno could hear a dispassionate voice reciting Article 38 of the Starsea Navigation Safety Act in her mind: Decommissioned vehicles are strictly prohibited on routes. But the big, dewy eyes of the furry little ones stared right through the voice and into her heart. "Write the ticket." Chen's voice fell without hesitation. Just as Harpeno was about to tear off the ticket, she paused and added, "Recommending referral to an animal shelter." "But, my shipment..." "You're an adult, so take responsibility for your actions like one," Harpeno didn't hesitate. "The cargo will be held in storage. Once the penalty is complete, you may retrieve it with a compliant vehicle." Lee accepted the ticket with eyes welling with tears.

On their way back, Chen gazed up at the sky of stars and said, "Remember this feeling. Rules are the backbone of the Starsea, but those who enforce them need to know what they're fighting for. You did the right thing today. You held the line and left room for compassion."

That night, Harpeno added a new entry to her log: "The Starsea needs order, but also, compassion."
She carefully folded the stub of the ticket for "No. 50" and tucked it away. Her uniform remained pressed and straight, yet somewhere between its rigid lines, Harpeno found a gentle give quietly forming.

"Are you pitying me?" She crumpled the map into a ball and tossed it back at Mo Ji. "I don't need directions from someone who can't even speak."
Mo Ji didn't get angry. She picked up the crumpled map, smoothed it out, then drew a large question mark on the back and held it out to her.
Harpeno let out a helpless laugh. In that instant, she knew she had gone too far.
"Sorry."
She left the word behind and turned away, eager to put an end to the conversation before it slipped any further out of her control.

And yet, Mo Ji soon began a strange kind of "communication" between them.
Whenever Harpeno deliberately went against the navigator's instructions, venting a frustration she couldn't quite name, a new map would appear in her locker the next day. Every wrong turn was marked in red, with a small stick figure doodled beside it, fuming with anger. She would scribble "Mind your own business" across the page. In reply, Mo Ji would sketch a girl covering her ears in the corner, neatly labeled: "Signal reception weak."

Gradually, Harpeno came to realize that Mo Ji's maps were more than routes. They were a language of their own. Color intensity indicated the severity of obstacles. Line weight marked their size. Vivid, concrete depictions made it easy to see what would otherwise be hard to picture. This was not something taught in textbooks. It was a private code, entirely her own.

The turning point came during the feared stardust belt navigation exam before graduation.
As Harpeno approached the target zone, the navigator began to glitch, and every instrument flickered wildly. Amidst the chaos at the exam control center, Mo Ji burst in, took the communicator, and made herself heard for the first time in three years—
"Trust your eyes, Harpeno!" Her voice was hoarse but steady. "Half a turn right. That nebula ahead isn't real. It's a debris field! Trust me. You can see it."
Harpeno held her breath. Her gaze pierced through the interference, and sure enough, there was a hidden safe passage. Mo Ji had already mapped the area in greater detail than any navigation system could. And in that moment, she chose to trust Harpeno's eyes over every instrument.

When the exam concluded, Harpeno found Mo Ji. "Why did you...?"
"My parents were Starsea cartographers," Mo Ji wrote slowly across the page. "They lost their way in the Starsea for lack of accurate charts, and never returned. I map the Starsea so no one else will be lost to the unknown. And you are..." She paused. "You're the only person I've ever met who can verify all my charts with the naked eye. I need your sight."

She did not see Harpeno as someone in need of saving. She was simply looking for someone to walk the same path.

At graduation, Mo Ji gave Harpeno one final Starsea chart.
"I'm going to finish what they started," Mo Ji said, "And you'll go on to build your own order."

Years later, the name of the Starsea Tyrant had spread far and wide, yet Harpeno never saw Mo Ji again. In the depths of her heart, however, there would always be a serene stretch of stars reserved for a certain "Starwhisperer."

After clocking out for the day, Harpeno went home and made herself a cup of coffee. Outside her window, the Starsea remained clamorous, but every route ran with orderly discipline. She tapped her fingertips lightly against the cup.
"And that's the way a peaceful night should be."

"YOU'RE INSANE!!!" He screamed.
"Now you know who catches the wind," she replied nonchalantly. "The black hole."
Harpeno's eyes and mind calculated the vehicle's trajectory with precision. When the drunk driver's survival instincts finally forced him to hit the brakes, she was already there to greet him at the only exit with a tap on his window.

"Two hundred percent over the speed limit, and driving under the influence to boot," she handed over the digital ticket. "You've just set a new record for violations in five years, and unfortunately, you'll be paying for your recklessness for the next five to come."

After the heart-racing, sobering chase, the man accepted the ticket with a ghastly white face. In that moment, the entire Starsea could hear the sound of his engine dying.

During Harpeno's final year at the Transit Academy, she was on the edge of erupting like a volcano every single day. Her hawkeyes could pierce through nebulas with ease, but she couldn't remember how to get from the lecture hall to the cafeteria to save her life.
"Worthless!" She slammed the electronic navigator onto the bench in frustration. "Did they design the path with their eyes closed?!"

A folded piece of paper slid to her feet. On it was a hand-drawn campus map, with each path marked by unique visual landmarks. "Turn left at the rusted car shell," "go straight past the café with the pigeon cage," and "turn right at the yellow-hatted scarecrow." The directions were precise, but peculiar.

She looked up and saw Mo Ji, the campus "weirdo" rumored to have not spoken a word in three years.
Mo Ji stared silently at her with eyes as calm as deep space.

Seasons passed, and Tika grew a little older.
She even achieved her dream and became... half a fruit farmer.

"I'm off to the orchard!"
Tika slung on her little backpack, stuffed with her small shovel and rake, and headed out. Lately, a bunch of agriculture students had been attending workshops at the orchard. Tika always tagged along, even if she hardly understood anything they said.
But planting trees? That she definitely knew how to do. You just dig a hole, place the sapling inside, and cover it with dirt again. She had even learned a new trick recently: you have to dig the hole a little deeper for trees.
"We work with fruit trees every single day in our major," one of the senior students told Tika while breaking up the soil with a rake. She was amazed by how much passion the little kid had for fruit trees. "If you want to plant fruit trees and don't mind the hard work, you should come study agriculture with us."
But who would ever think hanging out with fruit trees was hard work? Tika stood at the far end of the student group and puffed her chest out with pride.

It was okay if she didn't become a fruit farmer right away, because from that day forward, agriculture student Tika would grow every single one of those wondrous fruits from her dreams!

It's Tika's fourth year as an agriculture student. Out the gates of her beloved orchard, she steps into the Starsea alone, like a tiny seedling breaking through the soil.
She's going to cultivate all her ideas into fruits that are uniquely Tika, and prove their worth to everyone.

Professor Pablo is feeling rather troubled.
That difficult student of his, Tika, left a note behind and ran off somewhere.
"She says she's going to grow the most Tika-style avocados ever! What does that even mean? Is she going to plant seeds in a stone again and expect them to grow? It's utter nonsense!"
The little old man's beard bristles with frustration. He wants to call her immediately and drag her back here if he has to.
But his fingers hesitate over the dial. And then, he finally concedes and hangs up the receiver with a sigh. He grabs a pen and paper instead and pens a long, long letter, giving Tika advice on everything from cultivating techniques to how to take care of herself in her day-to-day life. The letter ends with a weighted but sincere, "Work hard, learn everything you can, and if you ever run into a problem you can't solve, you can always come back."

"Professor, do you even know Tika's address? Where are you going to send this letter?"
"...I said don't worry about it! It's just a draft! I'll call her later and read it to her!"

Today is her senior's graduation ceremony, and Tika's been invited by her to attend. However, the budding fruit farmer looks unusually downcast and completely drained of her usual energy. "What's wrong?" The senior crouches down and pats the little one's head. She's grown fond of Tika — the kid's smart and motivated, and kept her company through the most grueling days of writing her thesis. Tika's whimsical ideas never failed to make her laugh out loud. "Dina, I don't wanna be an agriculture student anymore." Oh no...! Is this really coming from Tika, the Tika who loved spending time with fruit trees more than anything? Dina's eyes widen, and her hand freezes in place. "What happened?" What did happen? Tika can't really explain it either, because she just can't put her head around why her teacher kept shooting down all her cultivation ideas. Her teacher said her ideas "violated the basic principles of plant growth." But how would he know they won't work for sure when he's never tried? "Dina, when will everyone stop treating my ideas as jokes...?" "I'm serious about them. I really wanna test every single one of them."

Starting today, I'm an agriculture student!
The teacher said I was granted a "special mission." I don't really get it. Nobody told me what the mission is.

People who love eating sugarcane nodes will definitely support me!

Teacher said nobody likes eating sugarcane nodes and told me to go back to working on fruit trees. Fruit trees are great, and I love spending time with them, especially Paltas!
I got a new idea to breed salty Paltas, or spicy ones. Someone might want to try bitter Paltas too. Anyway, it would be great if tasteless fruits like Paltas came in more flavors!
If only the teacher would let me, I'd breed Paltas in all kinds of colors, too. It's so boring that they're always the same color!
I'll get to work on it tomorrow! Gonna give it my all, heh heh.

Those are all the "right" answers. Tika looks at them carefully, one by one, but none of them catches her interest. Be a teacher?... No, no. The teacher can't even figure out what Tika's gonna be when she grows up. What about a scientist?... No, no. They wear baggy clothes and have crazy hair. "Tika dear, how about we go inside and play with your new doll?" "No! I want to plant saplings!" Tika's grip tightens. "Leave the planting to the grown-ups, Tika. Kids like you only have to worry about going to school and having fun." "Besides, the hole you dug is too shallow. Even if you planted the seeds, they wouldn't grow." All of a sudden, Tika feels herself being hoisted into the air and carried off. Ugh! Not this again! The grown-ups never believed that she's big enough to do these things. All she wanted was to plant some trees in the orchard with everyone else. She isn't trying to cause any trouble! Sure, she doesn't know how it grew out, b-but... that shows she's definitely not just playing around as the grown-ups have claimed! Tucked firmly under her parent's arm, Tika crosses her arms and tries her hardest to keep a stiff face. No jiggly cheek is going to stop her from making her serious protest clear today. Tika wants to play with the fruit trees. Tika is VERY unhappy!

Message from Home:
Tika's always been curious about everything! But honestly, she's probably just playing around, haha. She's only a kid. As long as she's having fun, that's all that matters for now.

Tika's not a slow child. In fact, she's the brightest kid in the orchard.
Fruit farmers there would always tell their kids, "Look at Tika! When are you going to get perfect scores like her?"
"But she couldn't even answer the teacher's question today!" one kid protests stubbornly, craning their neck and shouting loud enough for the whole orchard to hear.

Tika hears it too, but she pays it no mind. She sits in the shade of a tree and watches the farmers harvest fresh fruit. She sees how they climb the tall trees and catch the avocados freed from the branches with nimble snips of those pointed scissors.
It's super amazing!
Right now, Tika's still stuck with the round-tipped children's safety scissors, and she's barely the height of a young tree sapling. There's no way she can climb the towering avocado tree — it's almost as tall as the sun!
Tika looks up. The bright sun dazzles her eyes, leaving imprints of the farmers' silhouettes in her vision.
Getting to visit the orchard whenever you want and growing fruit trees however you please without anyone nagging you... Isn't that just what a fruit farmer does?

How could the years allotted by Heaven and Earth ever be borrowed? "If you carry compassion in your heart, you will see the soul in all living things." The immortal lowered her gaze, and the light that fell upon him was heavy with pity. But why? Why? Why must we be the ones to bear such cruel mercy? A child so young naturally could not understand. Yet someday... A sudden wind swept through the ancient book, turning page after page as the boundless ink slowly faded into nothingness. See not. Hear not. Know not... Form alone endures, and therein lies longevity... Why? Why? Why must we be the ones robbed of a home? They had promised. When spring came, we would go home. How did the wait for a single spring stretch into ten empty years? If only I could see them again. Just one last time... To look upon the pines of our home is to see us. Just one more glimpse. That was all I begged of the heavens... If you can't find your way home... promise me you won't cry.

"I don't want to feel anything." He heard the petulance in his own voice. To think he was once so willful, and that there had once been someone who simply let him be. "Those people bound to us by fate... they're all... they're all here to..."

"To 'borrow years' from us?" Sister Jiu suddenly laughed. But the frail laughter soon dissolved into a violent, unrelenting fit of coughing. The sound shook him to the core, setting his heart pounding with dread and leaving him scarcely able to breathe.

So the stories about borrowing years were true?
"To live or to die is but the natural course of things..." Her sigh stirred the flowing light. "Yet, most hearts in this world have nowhere to rest. And with nothing to hold on to, how is one to bear the weight of living? And so, they ask for the impossible."

Fleeing the southern winter, the young man cradled the sprig of red plum blossoms to his chest, carefully guarding it against the rocking of the boat that bore him toward home. 

To little Heyu, the journey felt agonizingly long. So long that the moment he closed his eyes, Sister Jiu would appear. He would see her leaning against the window, quietly unraveling the faded characters of an ancient book. And every time, he found himself burning to ask her: Why must our people live in hiding? Why is the road home so endlessly, unfathomably long?

"To keep from being found, of course." The memory, hazy and yellowed with time, suddenly found its voice. He realized with a pang that he had almost forgotten how she sounded. "That place... only those drawn by fate will ever find it. And when that moment comes, you will feel it, too."

The proprietor seemed to give in at last. His usual smile faded as he scratched ruefully at his ear and clicked his tongue once more.
"I see you've got rare aptitude. Fate must've put you in my path. And since you're here anyway... well, let nature take its course and see if you pull through."

On the path homeward, there stood a hot spring inn. Only upon sinking into its waters did he truly come alive.

The proprietor's eyes narrowed into a smile so forced that a vein throbbed visibly on his forehead. Grabbing the wretched lump by the collar, he dragged him inside and, with a casual heave, tossed him straight into the steaming pool.

"I couldn't care less if you have a home or not, just spare me the poetic nonsense!"

The ragged remains of his cloak slipped from him into the hot spring. Veiled in long white hair, the weakened young man fell to his knees, coughing uncontrollably until his palm was stained with blood.

Wedged between the snowy rocks lay a ragged heap of torn clothing, with fallen red plum blossoms scattered all around. The hot spring proprietor gave the... thing, which was presumably a person, a tentative nudge with his foot. "Hey there. Still alive, sir? We're running a hot spring here, y'know. A place for rest and recuperation. We don't do burials. So wherever you came from, best head on back!" The thing that was probably a person slowly raised its head. His face was deathly pale, his eyes as dull and vacant as a piece of shattered jade. Then, in a voice as cold as a ghost's, he said, "I have nowhere to return to."

Business was booming at The Named Springs, whose fame had spread far beyond the neighboring hills. Quite fittingly, it had made a name for itself.

"You really have an eye for location," remarked one of the guests as he soaked in the steaming water. "That legendary garden where the immortals are said to dwell is just a stone's throw away. No wonder these springs have something otherworldly about them."

The proprietor flicked his fan and gave a derisive snort. "When I first came out here to make a living, I'd never heard a peep about that garden. These springs owe what they are to nature. Gods, immortals, and all that lofty nonsense have absolutely nothing to do with it."

Just then, an old melon farmer came hurrying in, his face creased with worry. He'd spotted some strange-looking thing lying by the entrance, he said, and couldn't tell whether it was dead or alive. But if it had even a breath left, surely they couldn't just leave it there.

The proprietor paused, pinched his fingers together in a swift divination, and clicked his tongue. Snapping his fan shut, he rushed toward the door, leaving behind a muttered, "Just my rotten luck!"
When spring came, a new tale took root in the courtyard: the immortal had ascended and returned to the heavens.

Even in the dead of winter, the courtyard remained a riot of blossoms. It was absurdly lavish, reeking of an unnatural wealth. Rumor had it that a true immortal from the heavens was housed here.

"Some immortal, huh? Won't eat this, won't eat that. Picky as hell. Hardest creature I've ever had to serve."
"Even if he's a handful, you'll serve him on your knees! He's the Boss's living elixir for 'borrowing years.' Watch your tongue, or you'll get us in trouble!"
"Come on, you really believe something so bizarre? Borrowing someone's lifespan? I don't buy it..."
"How else do you explain it? How else do you explain it? Eight years ago, the Boss's only son was swallowed by a giant serpent. Everyone thought he was a goner. But look at him now, alive and kicking! You have to believe it."
"By the gods... So this isn't just 'borrowing years.' It's... going against Heaven and changing your fate!"
One man's face was riddled with doubt, while the other's was filled with awe.

Immortal? How absurd.
The aloof young man watched as lights suddenly flooded the courtyard, as if setting the jade halls and golden towers ablaze.

He pulled his hood low, snapped off a sprig of red plum blossoms, and stepped silently into the mountain mist.

The red plum Sister Jiu had planted... He had to bring it home. She always used to say the winters here were far colder than in their homeland. And that no matter what, he had to make it through, just until it was time to go home.

"Exactly! They say the Boss invited an immortal down to the mortal realm. As the immortal grows sickly and their life shortens, the Boss grows healthy and long-lived."
"I heard the older female lady only lasted a couple of years here before she... Wait, was it really because of that?!"
"Shh! Keep your voice down! You want to anger the one inside? We'll be doomed!"
"Oh, you're just being superstitious! What are you so scared of? It's been dead quiet in there. He must be asleep. He can't hear a thing..."

But were immortals not supposed to be omniscient? With a simple calculation on their fingers, they could see through an entire lifetime. The two men looked up at the sky in unison.

They say immortals are always watching from above. What if their careless words had already offended the one inside?

Uneasily, they pushed open the jade-inlaid window and looked toward the room bathed in moonlight—

Empty.

How could it be empty?!

Just as they did every year, the clan set sail once more. Lulled by the winds and waves of the Starsea, little Heyu drifted into a quiet sleep. As for what happened next... he couldn't quite remember.

When he finally opened his eyes, the ship had been moored at an unfamiliar planet. It was a garden of unnatural, suffocating extravagance. Sunlight spilled over endless, lavish layers of blooming flowers, growing so densely that they completely swallowed the path back.

Before he even had the chance to say goodbye, his people were already gone. Perhaps they had found somewhere else they preferred to spend the winter.

Thankfully, Sister Jiu was still there, holding his hand with a gentle smile.
"Don't be afraid, Young Master. When spring comes, we will go home."

Before long, the pavilion had filled with people, their voices rising in a lively hum. There was so much to pack. This one... or that one? Little Heyu furrowed his brow, unable to decide. He knew he was the frailest of them all, and that everyone had gone to such trouble for his sake. But it wasn't as though they were leaving forever. "We'll come right back when winter is over, won't we? We don't need to take so much with us." Silence settled over the pavilion. Then someone smiled. "I suppose you're right." One by one, they drifted back to their tasks. Outside, the autumn wind stripped the last lotus leaves from the pond. Only the pines remained.

"Would you like to bring this river lantern with you, Young Master?" "Mhm!" Little Heyu beamed, a smile sweet enough to melt the winter frost. "And what about this? The little porcelain sheep we made together. Shall we bring it too?" "Mhm!" He reached out and gently poked the little sheep held before him. "I think we'd better pack this quilt as well. He never sleeps well away from home." "Mhm!" Little Heyu wrapped both arms around it. So soft. "What for? It's so warm down south. He'll roast under that thing!" "Then how about this pillow?" "Or some canned peaches, for when you're sick?" "He'll need his cup for hot water, won't he?"

Every late autumn, the clan would depart for the warm south to spend the winter. Year after year, they traced the same path with the turning seasons, seeking only a place to rest.
This year should have been no different.

Inside the Plum Blossom Pavilion, the fire burned bright and warm. Wrapped in a mantle of soft brocade, little Heyu was little more than a fragile bundle, as warm and flawless to the touch as polished jade. The older youths of the clan busied themselves packing for the journey south. Yet, whenever they passed by him, they couldn't help but pause to steal a few moments with him.
